title: Relative clauses
intro: Relative clauses join two ideas. Use who, which, that, where and whose to say which person or thing you mean (B1) or to add extra information (B2).

sections.title: Defining relative clauses
sections.summary: A defining relative clause tells us which person or thing we mean. We cannot take it out without changing the meaning.

tables.caption: Relative pronouns
head: for
pronoun
example
rows: The woman who lives next door is a nurse.
The book that I bought was cheap.
That is the cafe where we met.
Do you remember the day when we met?
The man whose car was stolen called the police.
I know the reason why he left.

uses: Who is for people, which is for things, that can be used for both in a defining clause.
You can leave out the pronoun when it is the object of the clause: The film (that) we saw was great.
You cannot leave it out when it is the subject: The man who called was rude.
Do not use a pronoun twice: the book that I read it is wrong.
No commas are used in a defining clause.

examples.text: The student who won the prize is my cousin.
This is the shop where I bought my shoes.
The film we saw was great.
examples.note: The pronoun that is left out because it is an object.

mistakes.wrong: The man which lives here is kind.
mistakes.right: The man who lives here is kind.

mistakes.wrong: The book that I read it was long.
mistakes.right: The book that I read was long.

mistakes.wrong: She is the girl whose her bag was lost.
mistakes.right: She is the girl whose bag was lost.

checks.question: Join: I know a woman. She speaks five languages. (who)
checks.answer: I know a woman who speaks five languages.

checks.question: Complete: The house ___ we live is very old.

sections.title: Non-defining relative clauses
sections.summary: A non-defining clause gives extra information. Commas separate it from the rest of the sentence.

tables.caption: Defining and non-defining
head: type
example
that allowed?
pronoun can be left out?
rows: The boy who sits there is Tom.
Tom, who sits there, is my cousin.

uses: The noun is already clear without the clause: My brother, who lives in Leeds, is a doctor.
Use who or which, not that. Use whose, where and when too.
Use a comma before and after the clause. In speech you pause.
Which can refer to the whole clause: He passed the test, which surprised everyone.

examples.text: London, which is the capital of England, is very big.
Maria, whose husband is a pilot, works at the airport.
We went to Lisbon, where we met some old friends.
examples.note: Where adds extra information about a place.

mistakes.wrong: My mother, that is a nurse, works at night.
mistakes.right: My mother, who is a nurse, works at night.
mistakes.why: Do not use that in a non-defining clause.

mistakes.wrong: My car which is old broke down.
mistakes.right: My car, which is old, broke down.

checks.question: Complete: My sister, ___ lives in Rome, is a teacher. (who / that)
checks.explanation: That is not possible with commas.

checks.question: Complete: I live in Leeds, ___ is in the north of England. (that / which)
checks.explanation: Use which for extra information about a place name.
